name: Vikings
languages: Old Norse was the working language of the enterprise; the people who spoke it are described at the Norse article rather than here
religions: Participants were at first adherents of forn siðr, the pre-Christian Norse custom, which is why Latin and Old English sources call them pagans and heathen men rather than by any ethnic name
From the late tenth century the same activity was carried on by Christians: the conquest of England in 1016 was a Christian king's war

Nineteenth-century Romantic nationalist art is the myth this article exists to correct, so the page leads with the object that actually made the phenomenon possible and keeps Frank Dicksee's 1893 canvas far down the page, captioned as Victorian invention. The Gokstad hull is clinker-built of overlapping riveted planks, draws roughly a metre when loaded, and could be beached without a harbour or rowed far up a river — the technical facts behind every raid in this article. summary: Viking was something you did, not something you were. Old Norse víkingr named a man on a raiding voyage, and the Viking Age is a modern label for the period, conventionally 793 to 1066, when Scandinavians raided, traded, took service, explored and settled across an enormous span of coastline. The violence was real and well documented; the identity is a modern back-formation.
overview: An occupation that a nineteenth century mistook for a nation — and a campaign of raiding, extortion and slaving whose scale the correction must not soften.
knownFor: Named an activity, not a people: one went í víking, on a raiding voyage, and came home from it.
Opened with the sack of Lindisfarne in 793, which Alcuin of York described in letters written within months.
Turned raiding into conquest with the Great Heathen Army of 865, and conquest into rural settlement in the Danelaw.
Ran on silver and slaves, supplying the markets at Dublin and Hedeby and the Danegelds paid by Æthelred's government.
Acquired horned helmets, burning ship funerals and an ethnic identity between about 1820 and 1900, none of which are medieval.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: A víkingr was a man on a raiding voyage. That is the whole of the word's original meaning, and almost everything that has gone wrong in the popular understanding follows from forgetting it. Old Norse also had the feminine noun víking for the voyage itself: one went í víking and came back from it. This is vocabulary for an activity with a beginning and an end, not for who somebody is.

The people of common usage were Scandinavians — Danes, Norwegians, Swedes, Gotlanders, and later people of mixed Norse-Gaelic and Norse-Slavic descent — who between roughly 790 and 1100 used ships to take wealth from strangers, sell goods to strangers, hire themselves to foreign rulers, and settle land from Newfoundland to the Dnieper. They were not a nation, a tribe or a standing army, but the mobile, violent and commercially adventurous edge of a farming society, and the same man might raid one season, trade the next, and go home to get the hay in.

Two things have to be held at once. Ordinary Scandinavian life had nothing to do with raiding, so calling every Norse person a Viking is like calling every seventeenth-century Englishman a privateer. But the raiding was real, extraordinarily destructive, and documented in detail by the people it was done to: Alcuin of York was not inventing his distress in 793, monasteries were stripped, towns were burned, and tens of thousands of people were captured and sold. The correction to the horned helmet is not a pacified Viking. It is an accurate one.

This article covers the phenomenon: how it started, what made it possible, what it did, how it was resisted, why it wound down, and how it was remembered and then invented. The people who did it — their language, law, religion, farming, households and settlement — are covered at the Norse article.

contentSections.title: Names and Identity
paragraphs: Nobody who wrote about them called them Vikings. The victims reached for names of nationality, of religion, or of pure alarm: Dani and Nordmanni in Frankish and English sources, hæþene men and pagani in Old English and Latin, gaill — foreigners — in the Irish annals with the sub-labels Finngaill and Dubgaill, al-Majūs or fire-worshippers in Andalusi Arabic, Ascomanni or ash-men in Adam of Bremen, Rhos and Rūs in the east, and Varangoi for those in Byzantine service. Outsiders named them by where they came from or what they believed, never by what they were doing, because the word for what they were doing was the raiders' own.

The runic evidence for that word is worth setting out precisely. The Bro stone in Uppland, U 617, raised in the eleventh century by Ginnlaug, daughter of Holmgeirr, in memory of her husband Ôzurr, son of Jarl Hákon, says that he was víkinga vǫrðr. The phrase is genuinely there; its sense is not settled. It reads either as a guard against vikings or as a guardian of vikings, meaning their commander, and runologists have argued both. Either way, an eleventh-century Swedish family used the word in a martial phrase about somebody else's activity rather than about their own ancestry.

The Old English cognate is older than the Viking Age. The Épinal-Erfurt glossary, an English wordlist copied about 700 or at latest in the early eighth century and probably compiled at Canterbury a generation earlier, glosses Latin piraticum with the Old English compound wīcingsceáða, a piratical raider. The word was available in English for a sea-robber roughly ninety years before any Scandinavian fleet gave the English a reason to use it, which is decisive against reading it as an ethnic label.

The etymology is unresolved, and three proposals are worth setting against one another. The first derives it from vík, a bay or inlet — one who lurks in or comes from the bays — which runs into a difficulty of usage: the people of the Vík, the Oslofjord region, were called víkverjar, not víkingar. The second derives it from Old English wīc, itself from Latin vicus, a trading settlement, so that a wicing preys on trading places; this accounts for the early English attestation and allows the word to have travelled into Norse from English. The third connects it to víkja, to turn aside, either as a detour from a lawful voyage or, in a proposal Judith Jesch has developed, as a sense rooted in the mechanics of the sea voyage itself.

Viking as the name of a people is a nineteenth-century English development, running alongside the coining of vikingatiden, the Viking Age, in Scandinavian scholarship. The period label arrived with Romantic nationalism, which wanted ancestors, and the ethnic sense of the noun arrived with it. Every use of the Vikings to mean a population is a modern convenience.

contentSections.title: Why it began
paragraphs: Why then, and why so suddenly? There is no single answer, and the disagreement between the explanations is genuine. What can be said first is that it did not begin in 793. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that around 789 three ships came to Portland in Dorset and the king's reeve Beaduheard rode down to bring the crews to the royal estate, because he did not know what they were, and they killed him. Earlier still, at Salme on the Estonian island of Saaremaa, two ships buried around 750 held forty-one men, many with battle injuries, whose isotopes point to the Mälaren region of Sweden.

Technology is a necessary condition and not a sufficient one. The sail reached Scandinavia late — the fourth-century Nydam ship has no mast step, and Gotland's picture stones begin showing masted vessels only from around the seventh century. A sailing hull with a shallow draught turned the range of a Scandinavian crew from coastal to oceanic within a few generations, which explains how rather than why.

Silver supplies a why. Islamic dirhams begin arriving in the Baltic in quantity from the late eighth century, reaching Staraya Ladoga and then Gotland and Sweden, and James Barrett and others have argued that the eastern silver trade was the initial stimulus: it created an appetite for portable wealth and a class of men equipped to go and get it, and western raiding was in part that appetite pointed at a softer target. Demography supplies another: concubinage and partible inheritance produced more sons with claims than there was land to satisfy, and Barrett framed the resulting surplus of armed young men as a youth bulge — indirect evidence, but social logic well attested in the later law codes.

Politics is argued in both directions at once, and both may be true in different regions. One case holds that emerging royal power pushed the losers out, and Snorri Sturluson makes exactly this claim about Harald Fairhair driving men to Iceland, though he is a late and interested witness. The opposite case holds that the absence of strong central authority left war-band leaders free to act on their own account. Provocation and opportunity close the list: Charlemagne's conquest and forced conversion of the Saxons between 772 and 804 brought an aggressive Christian empire to the Danish border, and Danish rulers answered with fortification. Meanwhile the targets were extraordinarily soft. Monasteries stood on exposed coasts and islands, held concentrated metalwork, and had no defences. They were not chosen out of anti-Christian animus; they were the best-stocked undefended buildings in northern Europe.

contentSections.title: Lindisfarne, and what the sources say
paragraphs: The raid on Lindisfarne is the conventional beginning of the period, so it is worth setting out what the evidence consists of. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's annal for 793 opens not with ships but with omens: terrible portents came over Northumbria, immense whirlwinds and flashes of lightning, and fiery dragons were seen flying in the air, followed by a great famine — and then the heathen men miserably destroyed God's church on Lindisfarne with plunder and slaughter. The entry gives a date reading as 8 January, almost certainly a scribal error for 8 June, since a winter North Sea crossing is implausible, and the Chronicle was compiled about a century after the event.

The genuinely contemporary evidence is better and more disturbing. Alcuin of York, then at Charlemagne's court, wrote in 793 to King Æthelred of Northumbria and to Bishop Higbald of Lindisfarne. He describes the church of St Cuthbert spattered with the blood of its priests and stripped of its ornaments; he asks how such a thing could come to the place where the Christian faith in Britain began; and, being Alcuin, he tells the Northumbrians that their own sins and their taste for foreign hairstyles brought it upon them. These are letters written within months by a man who knew the place and the people in it.

There is also an object, carved on the island within a generation of the attack. A stone from Lindisfarne made between about 800 and 825, conventionally called the Domesday stone, shows on one face a row of men advancing with raised swords and axes, and on the other a cross with sun and moon and kneeling figures. Whether the carver meant the raiders of 793 or the Last Judgement cannot be settled from the stone, which is why it is useful: it shows what a Lindisfarne carver thought armed men looked like, without telling us what he meant by them.

Lindisfarne was not the first raid, as Portland and Salme show, and the reason it became the opening date of an era is that Alcuin was an internationally connected writer with a gift for alarm and the Chronicle was a text later readers trusted. The Viking Age begins in 793 because that is when the surviving literate world started writing the raids down at volume, not because anything changed at sea that year.

contentSections.title: The ship
paragraphs: Everything rested on one piece of technology. A Norse ship was clinker-built: overlapping planks, the strakes, riveted together edge to edge with iron rivets and caulked with tarred animal hair, forming a shell into which light internal framing was fitted afterwards. The result flexed with the sea instead of resisting it, and was very light for its size.

A shallow draught did the strategic work. The Gokstad ship draws roughly a metre loaded, which meant a crew could run the vessel up a beach and disembark without a harbour, and could work far up rivers — this is how fleets reached Paris on the Seine, moved up the Loire, and penetrated deep into Ireland and the Russian river systems. A keel and a mast step made sail possible on a flexible hull: the Gokstad's mast step is a massive block of oak, the kerling, which spreads the mast's load across several floor timbers, and the mast could be raised and lowered at sea. A side-mounted steering oar on the right-hand side gives English the word starboard.

Because such a ship needed no harbour, no coastal settlement was safe, and defending against it meant either fortifying everywhere or blocking the rivers — which is what Charles the Bald's Edict of Pîtres of 864 and Alfred the Great's system of fortified burhs set out to do, and why both eventually worked.

There was also more than one kind of ship, and conflating them produces the commonest picture-book error about the period. The five vessels scuttled about 1070 to block a channel in Roskilde Fjord and excavated in 1962 include Skuldelev 2, a warship of around thirty metres built near Dublin in 1042, and Skuldelev 1, a knarr: a broad, deep, high-sided sailing cargo ship. Raiders used the first type. The settlers who crossed to Iceland and Greenland with families, livestock and cargo used the second.

contentSections.title: How they fought
paragraphs: Not, for the most part, in battles. The characteristic operation was amphibious raid, extortion and withdrawal: arrive without warning, take portable wealth and people, and leave before a force could be gathered. When a fleet did stay, it built fortified camps and seized horses for mobility, which the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle notes with particular alarm because it removed the one advantage a defender had.

The best archaeological window on one of these armies is Repton in Derbyshire, where the Great Heathen Army wintered in 873 and 874. Excavation found a D-shaped earthwork incorporating the church, burials with weapons, and a charnel deposit of the disarticulated remains of at least 264 individuals, around eighty per cent male and mostly aged between eighteen and forty-five. Radiocarbon work published in 2018 confirmed the deposit as a single ninth-century event consistent with the army's presence. The winter camp at Torksey in Lincolnshire, in 872 and 873, covered some fifty-five hectares on the evidence of metal-detected finds — an encampment the size of a town.

In pitched battle there was nothing tactically exotic about them. They fought on foot in a shield wall, as at the Battle of Ashdown in 871, the Battle of Edington in 878, the Battle of Brunanburh in 937 and the Battle of Stamford Bridge in 1066, with spears in the front rank and missiles and insults before contact. At sea they did not manoeuvre or ram: fleets lashed ships together into fighting platforms and contested them like a field.

The scale of the violence should not be softened in the course of correcting the ethnic myth. Iona was attacked in 795, in 802, and again in 806, when sixty-eight members of the community were killed. Dorestad was sacked repeatedly from 834. Fleets took 7,000 pounds of silver to leave Paris in 845. The word entered half a dozen languages as a term of terror because of what was done with these ships, and an account that turns raiders into misunderstood merchants is as false as the horns.

contentSections.title: Atrocity, and the blood eagle
paragraphs: The blood eagle is the test case for how this archive handles an atrocity story. The earliest reference is a half-stanza in a skaldic poem, Sigvatr Þórðarson's Knútsdrápa of about 1038, which says that Ívarr caused an eagle to be cut on the back of Ella. That is the whole of the early evidence.

Later prose expands it enormously. Orkneyinga saga, Norna-Gests þáttr and Heimskringla, all thirteenth-century or later, develop the line into an elaborate ritual execution in which the ribs are cut from the spine and the lungs drawn out and arranged. Roberta Frank argued in an influential article of 1984 that this is a literary development rather than a practice: skaldic verse routinely uses the eagle as a carrion-bird image for a corpse left on a battlefield, so cutting an eagle on a man's back is most economically read as a kenning for killing him and leaving him to the birds, which later prose writers, no longer fluent in skaldic convention, literalised into surgery.

A study published in Speculum in 2021 examined the anatomical feasibility of the rite as the sagas describe it and concluded that it could in principle be performed on a dying or a dead body. That is a finding about anatomy and not about history: feasibility is not attestation, and no contemporary source describes anyone performing it.

This does not make the period gentle. The documented cruelties are of a different kind from the theatrical ones: the killing of sixty-eight monks on Iona in 806, the charnel deposit at Repton, the systematic taking of captives for sale. Those are attested by contemporaries and by excavation. The ritual with the ribs is attested by thirteenth-century Icelandic storytellers, and the difference between the two categories is the whole of the historical craft here.

contentSections.title: From war-band to royal war
paragraphs: The phenomenon had no organisation at all, and then it acquired one. Describing three centuries of Scandinavian seaborne activity as one thing is what produces the error of calling a king's invasion a raid.

In the first phase, roughly 790 to 850, the unit was the lið, a following raised by a leader who could feed and reward it. Fleets in the early annals are small — three ships at Portland, a handful on a coast — and leadership rested entirely on success, so a leader who stopped producing plunder stopped having followers. There was no strategy above the level of the individual voyage.

In the second phase, roughly 850 to 900, came the great armies. The force the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle calls the mycel hæþen here, the Great Heathen Army, landed in East Anglia in 865 and stayed for more than a decade: it took York in 866, killed Edmund of East Anglia in 869, wintered at Repton in 873 and 874, and divided so that part settled Northumbria and eastern Mercia while the rest went on. Armies of this kind were coalitions that combined and split, and they could hold territory, extract tribute and install kings. This is where raiding becomes conquest, and it is what produced the Danelaw and the Kingdom of York.

In the third phase, roughly 980 to 1070, came royal war. The Scandinavian attacks on England under Sweyn Forkbeard and Cnut the Great were organised by kings with national levies and fleets, aimed at a throne, and concluded with a coronation; Cnut then ruled England, Denmark and Norway as the North Sea Empire. These were not viking raids, and describing them as such flattens the century of political development that separates them from 865.

contentSections.title: West: Britain, Ireland and the Frankish rivers
paragraphs: The western theatre ran from opportunistic raiding to territorial conquest over about eighty years. Raids on the Northumbrian and Irish coasts began in 793 and 795; Frisia and the Frankish rivers followed, with Dorestad sacked repeatedly from 834. Paris was attacked in 845, when a fleet under a leader the Frankish sources call Reginherus took 7,000 pounds of silver to depart, and was besieged in 885 and 886 by a far larger force that Odo of Paris held off until the emperor Charles the Fat paid it away — a decision that cost him his throne and taught every Frankish magnate what tribute purchased.

Iberia was reached in 844, when fleets took Seville but failed against the citadel and were beaten by the forces of the Umayyad emir Abd al-Rahman II, who afterwards built ships and organised coastal defence. A second expedition of 859 to 862 passed the Strait of Gibraltar into the western Mediterranean. These were long-range ventures with no settlement behind them.

In England, raiding turned to conquest with the Great Heathen Army of 865 and to settlement with the Danelaw, where Scandinavian rural population is written into the map in place-names ending in -by, -thorpe, -thwaite and -toft — Grimsby, Whitby, Lowestoft, Braithwaite — and in a dense scatter of Scandinavian personal names attached to them. That is the signature of families farming, not of a garrison.

In Ireland the outcome was urban. Norse settlement produced the island's first towns — Dublin, founded as a longphort in 841, and then Waterford, Limerick, Wexford and Cork — and Norse dynasties became players in Irish politics rather than an external threat. Clontarf in 1014 is popularly told as Irish against Viking, and it was as much a contest between Irish over-kings, with Dublin's Norse and Leinster on one side and Brian Boru on the other. Its main narrative source, Cogad Gáedel re Gallaib, is a twelfth-century composition written to glorify Brian's descendants.

contentSections.title: East: the rivers, the Rus' and the Varangians
paragraphs: The eastern theatre was a different business: mainly commercial, conducted along rivers rather than coasts, and producing assimilation rather than any lasting Scandinavian identity. From Staraya Ladoga the routes ran to Novgorod and then either east down the Volga to the Bulgar market and the Caspian, or south down the Dnieper to Kyiv and Constantinople, which was attacked in 860.

What the eastern rivers moved was furs, wax, honey and above all people, exchanged for Islamic silver. The best outside descriptions come from Arabic writers who found the traders alien and said so: Ibn Fadlan met Rus' merchants on the Volga in 921 and 922, and Ibn Rusta described their settlement, their trade and their burial customs. Their value as evidence is that they owe nothing to either the Scandinavian or the Latin Christian tradition.

The Varangians deserve to be kept distinct from raiders. The word derives from vár, a pledge: these were sworn men in contracted foreign service. From 988, when Vladimir of Kyiv sent six thousand men to the emperor Basil II, they formed the Varangian Guard, the emperor's axe-bearing household troops. A Varangian was closer to a professional soldier under contract than to a man on a raiding voyage, and the careers connect the two worlds: Harald Hardrada served years in the Mediterranean in Byzantine pay before returning north to make himself king of Norway.

Politically the east produced Kievan Rus', by absorbing the newcomers rather than being conquered by them. The dynastic names shift language within three generations — Helgi, Helga and Ingvarr appear as Oleg, Olga and Igor, and Igor's son carries the Slavic name Svyatoslav — and by Vladimir's conversion in 988 the polity is Slavic and Orthodox. Nothing in the Rus' outcome resembles the Danelaw, and neither resembles Normandy.

contentSections.title: The North Atlantic
paragraphs: The third theatre was neither raiding nor trading but colonisation, mostly of land nobody held. The Faroes came first, then Iceland from about 870, then Greenland from 985 or 986 under Erik the Red, and briefly North America, where the turf buildings at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland were in use around 1021 — a date fixed to the year by matching the cosmic-ray spike of 993 in wood cut there with metal tools.

This is the part of the phenomenon that most thoroughly contradicts the popular image, because it required the opposite of a longship and the opposite of a war-band. Families crossed with livestock, seed, iron and tools in the knarr, a broad deep cargo hull that sailed rather than rowed. What they built were farms: turf-walled longhouses, home fields, summer pasture, and a dispersed settlement pattern with no towns in it at all.

The North Atlantic settlements also show what the enterprise looked like when the violence was absent and the economics were still ruthless. Greenland's export income rested overwhelmingly on walrus ivory, which tied several thousand people on the edge of the habitable world to a single luxury market in Europe. When African elephant ivory returned to that market in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries the colony's one commodity collapsed, a dependence that isotope work on walrus rostra in European collections has since confirmed.

Vinland was not a failure of nerve and was not a colony. The sagas that describe it, Grœnlendinga saga and Eiríks saga rauða, are thirteenth-century Icelandic literature about events of around 1000, and what the excavation at L'Anse aux Meadows shows is a base occupied briefly, with iron working and boat repair, rather than a settlement. A few dozen Norse Greenlanders several weeks from home, facing a populated continent, had no prospect of holding anything.

contentSections.title: Silver, tribute and slaves
paragraphs: What the phenomenon produced, materially, was silver and slaves. The silver arrives in the archaeological record as hoards: the Cuerdale hoard from Lancashire, deposited around 905 to 910 and containing some 8,600 objects, is the largest from western Europe; the Spillings hoard on Gotland, buried in the 870s, weighs about sixty-seven kilograms; and Gotland alone has produced roughly seven hundred hoards. Silver was weighed rather than counted, cut into hack-silver and balanced against standardised weights on folding scales.

Tribute was the most efficient form of extraction, because it required no fighting. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records a sequence of payments by Æthelred the Unready's government to buy off Scandinavian fleets: £10,000 in 991 after the English defeat at Maldon, £16,000 in 994, £24,000 in 1002, £36,000 in 1007, £48,000 in 1012, and a heregeld of £72,000 in 1018 with a further £10,500 from London alone. The figures come from a single hostile source and may well be inflated. The scale, however, has independent corroboration: tens of thousands of English silver pennies of Æthelred II have been recovered from Scandinavian soil, and more examples of some issues have been found in Sweden than in England.

Slaves were the other principal product, and the one routinely written out. Raiding produced captives and captives were sold. Dublin became one of western Europe's major slave markets within a few generations of its foundation as a longphort in 841, supplied by raiding in Ireland and Britain and selling on to the Continent and beyond; Hedeby handled the traffic at the base of Jutland; and on the eastern rivers the Rus' dealt in people as a staple, with Arabic geographers describing the flow of ṣaqāliba into the caliphates. The silver in the hoards and the people in the markets are two halves of one economy.

Trade proper used the same ships, the same men and the same routes, carrying furs, walrus ivory, amber, antler, soapstone, whetstones, wax and honey out, and bringing back silk, glass, wine, weapons and spices. The relationship between the two activities is mechanical rather than proverbial: a crew that could not sell what it took had no reason to take it, so the raiding depended on the market towns, and the market towns handled the proceeds of the raiding, including the people.

contentSections.title: Camps and towns
paragraphs: Raiding left camps, and they form a distinct archaeological class quite unlike a settlement. The longphuirt of Ireland, the D-shaped enclosure at Repton, the fifty-five-hectare winter camp at Torksey and the camp at Aldwark in Yorkshire are large, lightly built, and full of metalworking debris, gaming pieces, weights and cut silver. That assemblage is the material signature of an army processing plunder: melting it down, weighing it, dividing it and gambling over it.

The towns are different in kind. York's Coppergate excavations of 1976 to 1981 uncovered whole timber-lined tenements with their workshops and yards, and waterlogged deposits that preserved leather, wood and textile — the best picture anywhere of daily life in a Norse-ruled town, and a picture of cobblers, woodturners and jewellers rather than warriors. Dublin's Wood Quay produced a comparable sequence of plot boundaries and houses maintained over generations.

The contrast is the clearest physical evidence for the argument this article makes. A camp is temporary, defended, and full of other people's property. A town is permanent, laid out in plots, and full of manufacture. Both were made by the same population within a century of each other.

Full treatment of Norse building — the longhouse, turf construction, the ring fortresses of Harald Bluetooth, the dispersed farm settlement pattern — belongs at the Norse article, where it describes how these people lived rather than how they campaigned.

contentSections.title: How it was resisted
paragraphs: The resistance is better documented than the raiding and is the part of the story that explains the ending. Francia paid first and fortified second. Tribute bought departures repeatedly through the ninth century, which functioned as a subsidy to the industry, and Charles the Bald's Edict of Pîtres in 864 changed the approach: fortified bridges on the rivers to deny passage upstream, a prohibition on selling horses and arms to the Northmen, and organised local defence. By 911 the Frankish answer had become to settle a band of them on the lower Seine to keep the others out, which created the Duchy of Normandy.

England reorganised more systematically than anyone. Alfred the Great's response after the Battle of Edington in 878 was structural rather than heroic: a network of fortified burhs spaced so that no part of Wessex lay far from one, recorded in the Burghal Hidage; a rotation of the levy so that half the force was always available while the other half worked; and ships. His successors used the same tools to reconquer the Danelaw, and Æthelflæd of Mercia built burhs on the same model. A century later Æthelred's government reverted to paying, with the results recorded in the Danegeld figures.

Ireland absorbed rather than expelled. Norse settlement produced towns, and the Norse dynasties of those towns became participants in Irish dynastic politics — allies, rivals and in-laws — which removed the external quality of the threat without removing the violence. Byzantium simply hired them: rather than repel the northerners who attacked Constantinople in 860, the empire contracted them through the trade agreements of 907, 911 and 944 and then, from 988, the Varangian Guard.

The common feature of everything that worked is unglamorous. Walls, bridges, garrison rotas and contracts of employment defeated the longship, not battles. Once the coast was fortified and the rivers were blocked, a system built for undefended monasteries had nothing left to be aimed at, and the men who had crewed it were more valuable under contract than at large.

contentSections.title: Weapons, armour and the horned helmet
paragraphs: The equipment is described in full at the Norse article, and three points belong here because this is the page readers arrive at carrying the myths. The first is that most men fought with spear and shield rather than with a sword. Swords were expensive, and the best were imported Frankish blades — including the Ulfberht group, which reached Scandinavia in quantity despite the Carolingian prohibition on arms exports to the north in the Capitulary of Diedenhofen of 805.

The second is a matter of chronology that the popular image gets backwards. The great two-handed axe, the Dane axe wielded by the housecarls of Cnut and Harold Godwinson and shown repeatedly on the Bayeux Tapestry, is genuinely characteristic of Scandinavian warfare — but it belongs to the eleventh century, at the very end of the period, and not to the raiders who came ashore at Lindisfarne in 793.

The third is the horns. There were none. The only substantially preserved helmet from Viking-Age Scandinavia is the plain iron, spectacle-guarded helmet from Gjermundbu in Norway, from a grave of about 950 to 1000, and no Viking-Age find or contemporary depiction anywhere shows a horned war helmet. The horns were supplied by the nineteenth century: Carl Emil Doepler designed horned headgear for the costumes of the first complete Ring cycle at Bayreuth in 1876, with a generation of Romantic Scandinavian illustration already behind him. Horned helmets do exist in Scandinavia — the pair from Veksø in Denmark — but they are Bronze Age ceremonial objects roughly a thousand years older than any viking.

The rule to take from this section is that where a piece of Viking equipment is famous, its date should be checked. The sword is a status object rather than a standard one, the great axe is late, the horns are Victorian, and the spear that nearly everybody actually carried has almost no presence in the popular image at all.

contentSections.title: Religion and the raiders
paragraphs: The belief system belongs to the Norse article; only two points are specific to the phenomenon. The first is that the sources identify these men by religion because they had no other useful label: heathen men in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, pagani in Latin, al-Majūs in Arabic. When the victims of a raid cannot name the raiders' country, they name what the raiders are not.

Monasteries were targeted for their wealth and their defencelessness rather than as an assault on Christianity, though the ecclesiastical writers who recorded the attacks understood them as divine punishment for Christian sin — Alcuin says so explicitly in 793, and blames Northumbrian morals and hairstyles before he blames anybody from Scandinavia. That reading shaped the record permanently, because the men who wrote the surviving accounts were the professional victims of the phenomenon.

The second point is that conversion did not stop the activity, which is fatal to any account that treats the Viking Age as a pagan interlude ended by Christianity. Christian Scandinavian kings went on campaigning by sea throughout the eleventh century. By 1107 to 1110 Sigurd of Norway was leading a fleet to the Holy Land in an expedition that looks structurally like a viking voyage with a papal justification attached — the same ships, the same crews, the same pattern of coastal assault, differently licensed.

What conversion changed was the accounting. A Christian king with a kingdom wanted stable revenue, tithes and a place in European dynastic politics, and the naval levy that had carried raiders became a tax. The activity ended not because the gods changed but because the men who commanded the ships acquired something more profitable to do with them.

contentSections.title: Why it ended
paragraphs: It did not end at the Battle of Stamford Bridge in 1066. It wound down, over roughly two centuries, for reasons that can be named individually. The targets hardened first: burhs, fortified bridges, town walls and organised levies raised the cost of a raid and cut its returns, and a system built for undefended monasteries could not easily be re-aimed at fortified towns.

The money moved next. The flow of Islamic dirhams into the Baltic dried up in the later tenth century as the Central Asian mines faltered, restructuring the trade network that had helped generate the activity and reorienting Scandinavian attention toward English and German silver — which is part of why England was attacked again so heavily from about 980.

Then the raiders became kings, and kings prefer taxes to plunder. Once Scandinavian rulers governed territory they had an interest in predictable revenue, and Christianisation tied them into a European political and ecclesiastical order with its own norms about whom one may rob. In England the political option closed as well: the Norman Conquest replaced a Scandinavian-adjacent aristocracy with a Continental one and removed the Danish claim as a realistic proposition, though Sweyn Estridsson's fleets tried in 1069, 1070 and 1075.

And then it trailed on for two centuries anyway, which is the part the 1066 version hides. Magnus Barefoot campaigned in the Irish Sea until he was killed in Ulster in 1103. Norwegian rule in the Hebrides survived until the Battle of Largs in 1263 and the Treaty of Perth in 1266. The Northern Isles remained Norse-speaking and under Norwegian and then Danish sovereignty until 1468 and 1469. The neat end in 1066 is a convenience of narrative, chosen because Harald Hardrada's death makes a satisfying close.

contentSections.title: The Victorian invention
paragraphs: Almost the entire popular image was assembled between about 1820 and 1900 by Romantic nationalists in Scandinavia, Britain and Germany who wanted heroic ancestors and a usable pagan past. The individual components can be dated, and most of them to a decade.

The horned helmet dates from this period, as does the funeral pyre on a burning ship drifting out to sea — a scene with no basis whatever in the archaeology, which shows ships either buried in mounds or burned on land. Frank Dicksee's oil painting The Funeral of a Viking, exhibited in 1893 and now in Manchester Art Gallery, is the definitive image of a ceremony that appears never to have taken place in that form. Wagner's Ring, first staged complete at Bayreuth in 1876, fused Norse and continental German material into a single mythology in the public mind, and Carl Emil Doepler's costumes for it put horns on the result.

The most consequential invention was grammatical rather than visual. Viking, a word for something a man did for a season, was converted into the name of a people — and once it was a people it could be given a bloodline, a character and a destiny, which is what nineteenth-century nationalism wanted it for. Andrew Wawn's study of the Victorian reception traces the machinery in detail, and the machinery is still running: modern far-right movements use Viking imagery heavily, frequently with symbols that are not Viking-Age at all, such as the vegvísir, first attested in an Icelandic manuscript of 1860.

The evidence runs directly against that appropriation. The large population-genomics study of Viking-Age remains led by Eske Willerslev and published in 2020 found substantial gene flow into Scandinavia from the south and east, considerable diversity within Viking-Age populations, and individuals buried with full Scandinavian rites who had no Scandinavian ancestry at all. Crews were assembled from whoever would sail, which is what one expects of a job rather than a nation.
These paintings and operas remain excellent evidence. They are evidence for the nineteenth century, and treating them as evidence for the ninth is the single most common error a reader arrives with.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: What survived the phenomenon is mostly political geography. The Danelaw left several hundred English words and a map of northern and eastern England written in Scandinavian place-names. Ireland's port cities — Dublin, Waterford, Limerick, Wexford, Cork — exist because Norse fleets needed bases. The Duchy of Normandy, created in about 911 to keep other raiders out, produced the dynasty that conquered England in 1066 and, through it, changed the language and the landholding of a kingdom.

Further afield the results are just as concrete. Kievan Rus' took its name, and its first dynasty, from northerners who were speaking Slavic within three generations. Iceland and the Faroes were settled permanently and remain so. And the Atlantic was crossed five centuries before Columbus, a claim that spent a long time as a saga tradition and is now dated to the exact year 1021 by the wood cut at L'Anse aux Meadows.

Set against that is the word itself. Víkingr entered other European languages as a term for a seaborne raider, then in the nineteenth century was converted into the name of a people it had never named, so the most durable product of the Viking Age is a mistake about it. The Norse article covers what those people actually were; this page exists to keep the distinction visible, because a word that names an occupation cannot also name an ancestry.

The final legacy is methodological. Almost every popular certainty about the Vikings turns out on inspection to be either a thirteenth-century Icelandic literary invention or a nineteenth-century national one, while the genuinely secure knowledge — the ships, the camps, the hoards, the tree-ring date in Newfoundland, the isotopes in Greenland walrus ivory — has come from excavation and laboratory work, much of it within living memory. The evidence is still moving, and it has consistently moved against the myth.

timeline.title: The Salme ship burials
timeline.description: Two ships buried on the Estonian island of Saaremaa hold forty-one men, many with battle injuries, whose isotopes point to the Mälaren region of Sweden. Organised Scandinavian seaborne violence four decades before Lindisfarne.

timeline.title: Three ships at Portland
timeline.description: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that a royal reeve named Beaduheard rode down to Portland to bring the crews to the king's estate, because he did not know what they were, and was killed.

timeline.title: Lindisfarne
timeline.description: The monastery is sacked, and Alcuin of York writes within months to King Æthelred of Northumbria and Bishop Higbald describing the church of St Cuthbert spattered with the blood of its priests. The conventional opening of the Viking Age.

timeline.title: Iona attacked three times
timeline.description: The island monastery is raided repeatedly, and in 806 sixty-eight members of the community are killed. The survivors moved the community's treasures inland to Kells.

timeline.title: Dorestad sacked repeatedly
timeline.description: The great Frisian emporium on the Rhine delta is attacked year after year, demonstrating that a wealthy trading town with no walls was as soft a target as a monastery.

timeline.title: A longphort at Dublin
timeline.description: A fortified ship camp is established on the Liffey. Within a few generations it is one of western Europe's principal slave markets and Ireland's first town.

timeline.title: Seville taken
timeline.description: Fleets sack the city but fail against the citadel and are defeated by the forces of Abd al-Rahman II, who afterwards builds ships and organises coastal defence against a repeat.

timeline.title: Paris raided
timeline.description: A fleet under a leader the Frankish sources call Reginherus reaches Paris on the Seine and takes 7,000 pounds of silver to depart — the clearest early demonstration that tribute was more profitable than fighting.

timeline.title: Constantinople attacked
timeline.description: Northerners from the Rus' river routes assault the imperial city. The empire's eventual answer was not to repel them but to contract them, through trade agreements and then military service.

timeline.title: The Edict of Pîtres
timeline.description: Charles the Bald orders fortified bridges on the Frankish rivers to deny passage upstream, and forbids the sale of horses and arms to the Northmen. The template for every defence that worked.

timeline.title: The Great Heathen Army
timeline.description: The force the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle calls the mycel hæþen here lands in East Anglia and stays more than a decade, taking York in 866 and killing Edmund of East Anglia in 869. Raiding becomes conquest.

timeline.title: The Great Army winters at Repton
timeline.description: A D-shaped earthwork incorporating the church, weapon burials, and a charnel deposit of at least 264 individuals, confirmed by radiocarbon work published in 2018 as a single ninth-century event.

timeline.title: Edington
timeline.description: Alfred defeats Guthrum, who accepts baptism, and the partition that follows creates the Danelaw. Alfred then rebuilds Wessex around fortified burhs and a rotated levy.

timeline.title: Paris besieged
timeline.description: A far larger fleet invests the city, Odo of Paris holds it, and the emperor Charles the Fat buys the besiegers away — a decision that destroyed his standing and hardened Frankish policy against paying.

timeline.title: Rollo settled on the Seine
timeline.description: Charles the Simple comes to terms with a Scandinavian leader on the lower Seine, creating what becomes the Duchy of Normandy. No text of the agreement survives; the fullest account is by a panegyrist writing a century later.

timeline.title: Brunanburh
timeline.description: Æthelstan defeats a coalition including Norse-Gaelic forces from Dublin, checking the attempt to restore Scandinavian rule in York from the Irish Sea.

timeline.title: Eric Bloodaxe driven from York
timeline.description: The last Scandinavian king of York is expelled and killed, ending independent Norse rule in Northumbria. Scandinavian settlement in the north of England continued regardless.

timeline.title: The Varangian Guard formed
timeline.description: Vladimir of Kyiv sends six thousand men to Basil II, and they become the emperor's axe-bearing household troops — sworn men under contract rather than raiders.

timeline.title: Maldon and the first Danegeld
timeline.description: After an English defeat at Maldon, Æthelred's government pays £10,000 to buy off the fleet, beginning a sequence of payments that reached £48,000 by 1012.

timeline.title: Sweyn Forkbeard and Cnut take England
timeline.description: Kings with national levies and fleets conquer a kingdom and are crowned. These were royal wars aimed at a throne, not viking raids, and the distinction matters.

timeline.title: L'Anse aux Meadows occupied
timeline.description: Wood is cut with metal tools in Newfoundland, dated to the exact year by the 993 cosmic-ray spike in the tree rings — the only absolute date for a European presence in the Americas before Columbus.

timeline.title: Stamford Bridge
timeline.description: Harald Hardrada is killed in Yorkshire, which later convention made the end of the Viking Age. Nothing actually ended: Danish fleets attacked England again in 1069, 1070 and 1075.

timeline.title: Magnus Barefoot killed in Ulster
timeline.description: A Norwegian king dies campaigning in the Irish Sea nearly forty years after the supposed end of the period, in an expedition indistinguishable in form from those of two centuries earlier.

timeline.title: Largs and the Treaty of Perth
timeline.description: Norwegian sea power in the Hebrides is checked and then surrendered by treaty, ending Scandinavian rule in the Isles two centuries after the conventional close of the Viking Age.

sectionImages.section: Lindisfarne, and what the sources say
sectionImages.caption: The Domesday stone from Lindisfarne, carved between about 800 and 825 and photographed in 2022. One face shows a row of men advancing with raised swords and axes.
sectionImages.creator: Photographed 2022 (Wikimedia Commons); carver unknown
sectionImages.date: photographed 2022; the carving made between about 800 and 825
sectionImages.note: A contemporary object from the place where the story conventionally begins, carved on the island within a generation of the raid of 793. Whether the advancing men are the raiders or a Last Judgement scene is genuinely disputed and cannot be settled from the stone, which is why it is useful evidence: it shows what a Lindisfarne carver thought armed men looked like without telling us what he meant by them. Colour, high resolution, the stone filling the frame. Released CC0.

sectionImages.caption: Part of the Cuerdale hoard in the British Museum — coins and cut-up silver buried in Lancashire around 905 to 910, the largest Viking silver hoard from western Europe.
sectionImages.creator: Photographed for Wikimedia Commons (British Museum)
sectionImages.date: the silver deposited around 905 to 910; photographed for Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: About 8,600 coins and pieces of hack-silver, found near Preston in 1840. The hoard is the clearest physical statement of what the phenomenon produced: bullion weighed rather than counted, cut into fragments and balanced against standardised weights, and accumulated from raiding, tribute and the sale of captured people. Colour, silver filling the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.

sectionImages.caption: Frank Dicksee's oil painting The Funeral of a Viking, exhibited in 1893 and now in Manchester Art Gallery. The blazing ship pushed out to sea is a Victorian invention, not a Norse rite.
sectionImages.creator: Frank Bernard Dicksee (1853–1928)
sectionImages.note: Placed deliberately low in the article and captioned as myth rather than evidence. Norse ship burials were buried in mounds or burned on land, and no medieval source describes a burning vessel pushed out to sea; the painting is evidence for Victorian ideas about the Viking Age and for nothing about the ninth century. At 800 by 492 pixels it is adequate as a section image and would not have been acceptable as a lead, which it must never be on this page in any case. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: The Tjängvide picture stone from Alskog on Gotland, carved about 800 and photographed in 2008. Its lower panel shows a ship under a chequered sail with the crew aboard.
sectionImages.creator: Berig (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 1 March 2008; the stone carved about 800
sectionImages.note: A contemporary Scandinavian image of the thing this article is actually about: a crewed sailing ship, carved by people who used them, rather than a nineteenth-century painting of one. The upper panel shows a rider on an eight-legged horse, usually read as Odin on Sleipnir, being met by a figure with a drinking horn. The red pigment is modern conservation infill applied to make the relief legible, not original colour. Colour, the stone filling the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

sectionImages.caption: The Bro runestone, U 617, in Uppland, Sweden, raised in the eleventh century and photographed in 2007. Its inscription calls Ôzurr víkinga vǫrðr, either a guard against vikings or their commander.
sectionImages.creator: Berig (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 29 June 2007; the stone raised in the eleventh century
sectionImages.note: The single runic attestation this section turns on, and the reason the word cannot be read as an ethnic label. Ginnlaug, daughter of Holmgeirr, raised it for her husband Ôzurr, son of Jarl Hákon; the phrase víkinga vǫrðr is genuinely on the stone, but whether it honours him for fighting raiders or for leading them is unsettled among runologists, and this article does not pretend otherwise. Either way the word describes an activity, and somebody else's. Colour, the stone filling the frame. Licensed CC BY 2.5.

sectionImages.caption: The Nydam boat, an oak rowing vessel of about 320 from southern Jutland, photographed in 2015 at Schloss Gottorf in Schleswig. It has no mast step: a Scandinavian ship from before the sail.
sectionImages.creator: Holger Ellgaard (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 16 May 2015; the boat built about 320
sectionImages.note: The negative evidence behind this section's argument about timing. Scandinavians had large, well-built plank boats four centuries before Lindisfarne, and this is one of them — deposited in a bog as a war offering and recovered in the nineteenth century — but it was rowed, not sailed, and its range was therefore coastal. The sail is the change that converts an existing shipbuilding tradition into an oceanic one, which is why technology explains how rather than why. Colour, the hull filling the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

sectionImages.caption: Skuldelev 1, a knarr cargo ship built in Norway about 1030, photographed in 2017 at the Viking Ship Museum in Roskilde. This is the broad, deep sailing hull that carried settlers, not a longship.
sectionImages.creator: Colin (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 18 August 2017; the ship built about 1030 and scuttled about 1070
sectionImages.note: The correction this section makes, in physical form. Skuldelev 1 is one of five vessels scuttled about 1070 to block a channel in Roskilde Fjord and excavated in 1962; the same find produced Skuldelev 2, a thirty-metre warship built near Dublin in 1042. Seen from above, the depth of hull and the breadth amidships are exactly what a longship does not have, and what carrying families, livestock and cargo across the Atlantic required. Colour, the whole hull in the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

sectionImages.caption: St Wystan's church at Repton in Derbyshire, photographed in 2012. The Great Heathen Army wintered here in 873 and 874 and built a D-shaped earthwork that used the church itself as a gateway.
sectionImages.creator: Photographed for the Geograph Britain and Ireland project
sectionImages.date: photographed 27 October 2012; the Anglo-Saxon crypt of the eighth century
sectionImages.note: The best-excavated winter camp of the period, and the reason this section can describe how an army behaved rather than only how it fought. Excavation found the earthwork, weapon burials, and a charnel deposit of at least 264 people, about eighty per cent of them male and mostly aged eighteen to forty-five, confirmed by radiocarbon work published in 2018 as a single ninth-century event. The spire and upper church are later medieval; the crypt beneath is Anglo-Saxon and stood when the army arrived. Colour, the building filling the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 2.0.

sectionImages.caption: The Stora Hammars I picture stone from Lärbro on Gotland, carved in the eighth century and photographed in 1994 at the Bunge open-air museum. One panel carries the scene sometimes read as a blood eagle.
sectionImages.creator: Bengt A. Lundberg, Swedish National Heritage Board
sectionImages.date: photographed 29 August 1994; the stone carved in the eighth century
sectionImages.note: The image most often produced as evidence for the rite, and it illustrates this section's point rather than settling it: a figure lies face down while another stands over him and a bird hovers, which has been read as a blood eagle and equally as a sacrifice to Odin or a scene of ordinary killing. Nothing on the stone is captioned, and the reading is imposed by readers who already know the saga story. The stone stood at Lärbro and is now displayed at the Bunge museum, which is why heritage records file it under Bunge. Colour, the carving filling the frame. Licensed CC BY 2.5.

sectionImages.caption: King Cnut and Queen Emma presenting a gold altar cross to the New Minster at Winchester, drawn about 1031 in the New Minster Liber Vitae. A Danish conqueror depicted as a Christian king of England.
sectionImages.creator: Anonymous English artist of the eleventh century
sectionImages.source: Wikimedia Commons (British Library, MS Stowe 944, folio 6r)
sectionImages.note: The end state of the third phase this section describes, drawn within Cnut's own lifetime and only fifteen years after his conquest. He wears a crown and carries a sword but is shown endowing an English monastery beside his queen, with Christ and angels above and the monks of the community below — the iconography of a European monarch, not of a raider. Emma, Æthelred the Unready's widow, had married the conqueror of her first husband's kingdom. Colour, the page filling the frame. Public domain.

sectionImages.section: West: Britain, Ireland and the Frankish rivers
sectionImages.caption: A modern map, drawn in 2008, of the Danish Great Army's campaigns in England between 892 and 896, showing the Danelaw boundary agreed in 886 and the Anglo-Saxon burhs built against it.
sectionImages.creator: S. Bollmann (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.note: The western theatre at the moment raiding had become territorial: the Danelaw as a bloc, the Five Boroughs, Wessex and Mercia beneath it, and the campaign routes of 892 to 896 looping across all three. The burhs marked as dots are the fortress network that made those campaigns unprofitable, which is the subject of the later section on resistance. The legend is in German and the map is compiled from Graham-Campbell, Price, Logan, Sawyer, Keynes and Downham; the place-names are the familiar English ones. Colour, legible at section size. Licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.

sectionImages.section: East: the rivers, the Rus' and the Varangians
sectionImages.caption: The Piraeus Lion outside the Venetian Arsenal, photographed in 2007. Carved in Greece in antiquity, it carries a long runic inscription cut into its shoulders by Scandinavians in Byzantine service.
sectionImages.creator: Photographed for Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.date: photographed 8 April 2007; the runes cut in the eleventh century
sectionImages.note: Physical proof of the eastern careers this section describes, and of how far they reached. The lion stood at the harbour of Piraeus until Venetian forces carried it off in 1687; the lindworm-shaped runic bands on its flanks were cut by northerners serving the emperor, and are badly weathered but still visible in raking light. They are the same phenomenon as the Halfdan graffiti in Hagia Sophia: men from the Baltic leaving their names on Mediterranean stone. Colour, the sculpture filling the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 2.0.

sectionImages.caption: The entrance to a reconstructed turf building at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, photographed in 2010. Turf blocks are stacked in herringbone courses around a timber frame, as the Norse built them.
sectionImages.creator: D. Gordon E. Robertson (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 5 July 2010; a modern reconstruction beside the excavated site
sectionImages.note: A reconstruction rather than a surviving building — what remains of the originals is the outline of turf walls in the grass — but it shows the construction method that made the North Atlantic habitable and is the only known European building technique on the American continent before Columbus. Wood cut here with metal tools has been dated to exactly 1021 by matching the cosmic-ray spike of 993 preserved in the tree rings. Colour, the structure filling the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.

sectionImages.caption: A costumed interpreter striking coins in the reconstructed Coppergate street at the Jorvik Viking Centre in York, photographed in 2004. The excavated tenements held craftworkers rather than warriors.
sectionImages.creator: CambridgeBayWeather (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 11 February 2004; a modern museum reconstruction
sectionImages.note: A modern museum reconstruction, built over the Coppergate excavations of 1976 to 1981 and based on them. The waterlogged deposits there preserved leather, wood and textile along with the timber-lined tenements, giving the fullest picture anywhere of daily life in a Norse-ruled town — and the picture is of cobblers, woodturners, jewellers and moneyers, which is this section's whole contrast with the camps. Colour, the figure and workbench large in the frame. Licensed CC BY 2.5.

sectionImages.caption: The earth ramparts of the Anglo-Saxon burh at Wareham in Dorset, photographed in 2005. Wareham is one of the fortresses listed in the Burghal Hidage, the record of Alfred the Great's defensive network.
sectionImages.creator: John Lamper (Wikimedia Commons / Geograph)
sectionImages.date: photographed 19 November 2005; the ramparts raised in the ninth century
sectionImages.note: The unglamorous thing that actually worked. Wareham sits between two rivers on the south coast and its ninth-century bank still runs around three sides of the town; the Burghal Hidage assigns each burh a garrison calculated from the length of wall it had to man. A raiding system built for undefended monasteries had no answer to earthworks like this one, backed by a rotated levy that kept half the force available at all times. Colour, the rampart and ditch filling the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 2.0.

sectionImages.section: Weapons, armour and the horned helmet
sectionImages.caption: The horned bronze helmets from Veksø in Denmark, made about 900 BC and photographed in 2011 at the National Museum in Copenhagen. These are Bronze Age ceremonial objects, not Viking equipment.
sectionImages.creator: Simon Burchell (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 11 March 2011; the helmets made about 900 BC
sectionImages.note: The only genuinely horned helmets Scandinavia has produced, and they predate the Viking Age by roughly a thousand years — closer in time to Stonehenge than to Lindisfarne. Found in a bog at Veksø in 1942, they are thin sheet bronze and ceremonial rather than protective. Set against them stands the one substantially preserved Viking-Age helmet, the plain spectacle-guarded iron cap from Gjermundbu, which has no horns of any kind. Colour, the objects large in the frame behind museum glass. Licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.

sectionImages.caption: The bronze figure from Eyrarland in Iceland, cast about 1000 and photographed in 2012 at the National Museum of Iceland. The seated man grips a hammer-shaped object, read as Thor or as a Christian cross.
sectionImages.creator: L3u (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 21 August 2012; the figure cast about 1000
sectionImages.note: An object from precisely the moment this section describes, and unresolvable in precisely the useful way. Cast around the year Iceland voted to accept Christianity, the seated figure holds something that reads equally as Thor's hammer Mjǫllnir and as a cross, and scholars have argued both. That ambiguity is the evidence: conversion was a change of accounting and allegiance rather than a clean break, and the same fleets sailed after it. Colour, the object large on a plain ground. Licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.

sectionImages.caption: Borgund stave church in Lærdal, Norway, built about 1180 and photographed in June 2013. By this date the men who commanded Norway's ships were Christian kings with tithes to collect.
sectionImages.creator: Ximonic (Simo Räsänen)
sectionImages.date: photographed 18 June 2013; the church built about 1180
sectionImages.note: What the ending actually looked like, a century after Stamford Bridge: timber and carpentry of the same tradition that built the ships, turned to a parish church in a kingdom with a diocesan structure, a written law and a tax. The naval levy that had carried raiders had become a revenue system, which is this section's argument about why the activity stopped paying. Colour, the whole building in the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.

sectionImages.caption: Reginald's Tower in Waterford, Ireland, photographed in 2013. The stone tower is thirteenth-century and stands on the corner of the defences of the Norse town founded on this site in the tenth century.
sectionImages.creator: Photographed for the Geograph Britain and Ireland project
sectionImages.date: photographed 6 July 2013; the tower built in the thirteenth century
sectionImages.note: The most durable legacy named in this section is a map rather than a memory: Ireland had no towns before Norse fleets needed bases, and Dublin, Waterford, Limerick, Wexford and Cork all begin as ship camps. The masonry here is later than the Norse settlement and the tower takes its name from Ragnall, the Norse founder recorded in tradition, so it marks the site rather than surviving from it. Colour, the tower filling the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 2.0.
